overview:
The LORD tells Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month, put each piece in its place, and anoint the tent, its furniture, and Aaron and his sons. On that day of the second year out of Egypt, Moses does it: frames and tent, the testimony in the ark, the veil, table and bread, lampstand, incense altar, door hanging, the altar with its first offering, the laver, and the court. “So Moses finished the work.” Then the cloud covers the tent and the glory of the LORD fills it, so that Moses cannot go in. From then on the cloud by day and fire by night lead Israel's journeys.

The book ends where its story has been heading. Israel began Exodus building store cities for Pharaoh (1:11). It ends having built a dwelling for the LORD, and he moves in: the glory that rested on Sinai (24:16) now travels with the camp.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign the tabernacle chapters (25–31, 35–40) to a later priestly writer.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The first day of the first month of the second year after the Exodus (v. 17), about nine months after arriving at Sinai (19:1). On a 1446 BC Exodus, c. 1445 BC.

historicalContext.label: First audience
historicalContext.text: Israel, whether in the wilderness (traditional view) or after the exile, waiting for God's glory to return to a rebuilt temple (common scholarly view).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The camp at the foot of Mount Sinai, where Israel stays until the cloud lifts in Numbers 10:11.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Numbers 9:15–23 retells the cloud over the tabernacle; Leviticus 8 carries out the anointing of vv. 9–15. Compare the dedication of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10–11).

hermeneutics:
Temple-building stories in the ancient Near East follow a pattern: a god commands, materials are gathered, the house is built, and the god moves in. The fullest example is the cylinders of Gudea, ruler of Lagash (c. 2100 BC), on the temple Eninnu. When the work is done, the text says, a year ended and a new year began, and in its first days the god Ningirsu entered his house like a storm, followed by days of feasting. Exodus 25–40 follows the same outline, down to the new-year date (vv. 2, 17). The difference is what enters. Mesopotamian gods lived in their temples through cult statues; Exodus brings in no image at all, only a cloud and a glory too strong for Moses to approach (v. 35).

The first thing Moses puts in the ark is “the testimony” (v. 20), the tablets of the covenant (31:18). Hittite treaties of the 14th and 13th centuries BC were stored the same way. The treaty between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma and Shattiwaza of Mitanni says a copy was deposited before the storm god Teshub, and it was to be read aloud at set times. Placing the covenant document in the most holy place, under the mercy seat, put the agreement before the divine king who would hold Israel to it. Deuteronomy 31:9–13, 26 later adds the public reading.

structure.summary: Parallel panels: the LORD's command (vv. 2–8) and Moses' execution (vv. 17–33) in the same order, then the glory. Not a chiasm.

open.text: And the LORD spake unto Moses

close.text: The cloud covers; the glory fills; the cloud leads

notes: **Seven refrains:** “As the LORD commanded Moses” ends seven steps of the setting up (vv. 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 32), after a summary in v. 16. The pattern matches the seven refrains of the garments in ch. 39.
**A command held over:** The anointing of vv. 9–15 has no matching panel. It is carried out in Leviticus 8, when Aaron and his sons are ordained.
**Finished:** “So Moses finished the work” (v. 33) uses the verb and noun of Genesis 2:2, “God ended his work.” The glory then fills the tent, as the seventh day followed the finished creation.

Chapter 40 closes the unit begun in ch. 35 and the book. Chapters 35–39 made the pieces; here they are assembled, and the LORD takes up residence, fulfilling “that I may dwell among them” (25:8; 29:45).

**Looking ahead:** Leviticus opens with the LORD calling to Moses from this tent (Leviticus 1:1), and Numbers 9:15–23 expands vv. 36–38. When Solomon's temple is dedicated, the cloud fills the house and the priests cannot stand to minister, as Moses could not enter here (1 Kings 8:10–11).

traditions.text: The revelation on priesthood begins by promising a house built to the Lord in that generation, on which “a cloud shall rest,” a cloud that is the glory of the Lord filling the house. It also says the Lord confirmed a priesthood on Aaron and his seed throughout all their generations, the language of v. 15. The scene of this chapter becomes a promise for a latter-day temple.

The Lord promises that if his people build him a house and let nothing unclean enter it, his glory will rest on it and his presence will be there. If it is defiled, he will not come. The glory of v. 34 is offered again, but on a condition the tabernacle story leaves implicit.

At the dedication of the Kirtland Temple, Joseph Smith prayed that the Lord's glory would rest on the house and fill it “as with a rushing mighty wind.” A week later the Lord appeared in the temple and declared that he had accepted the house and would manifest himself there. Latter-day Saints read the occasion as a modern counterpart to the glory filling the tabernacle.

Josephus says the building took seven months and the tabernacle was consecrated at the new moon of Nisan, which the Macedonians call Xanthicus. He then softens the cloud of v. 34: under a clear sky a mist settled over the tabernacle alone, not so thick as a winter cloud nor so thin that one could see through it, and from it fell a sweet dew. The presence of God, he says, was evident to those who desired and believed it.

A teaching on v. 17 says that day “took ten crowns.” It was the first day of the week and of the month, the first day of the priesthood and of the service, the day fire first came down on the altar, the Shekhinah first rested on Israel, and the priests first blessed the people. From then on, offerings on private altars were forbidden.

Rashi sets v. 35 beside Numbers 7:89, where Moses does enter the tent to hear God speak. Following an old rule of interpretation, he lets the end of v. 35 resolve the conflict: Moses could not enter while the cloud rested on the tent, but could once it lifted. On v. 29 he adds that during the seven days of ordination Moses set the tabernacle up and took it down again, serving as priest himself.

This Aramaic paraphrase gives each anointing in vv. 9–11 a future meaning. The tabernacle is anointed for the crown of the house of Judah and the King Messiah who will redeem Israel at the end of days; the altar for Aaron's priesthood and Elijah, the great priest to be sent at the end of exile; the laver for Joshua and the Messiah son of Ephraim. The setting up of the sanctuary becomes a pledge of final redemption.

Ramban explains why Exodus ends with the tabernacle and not with the crossing of the sea or Sinai. Israel left Egypt but was still in exile, wandering in a land not its own. Only when the Divine Presence came to dwell among them again, as it had rested on the tents of the patriarchs, were they restored and the redemption complete.

After telling how Jeremiah hid the tabernacle and the ark, the letter promises that when God gathers his people, “the glory of the Lord shall appear, and the cloud also,” as it was shown under Moses and at Solomon's dedication. The cloud of this chapter becomes the sign of a future restoration.

John says the Word became flesh and “dwelt among us,” using a Greek verb built on the word for tent, and adds “we beheld his glory.” Tent and glory are the two terms of vv. 34–35. For John the presence that filled the tabernacle now lives in a human body.

The Greek Exodus says the cloud “overshadowed” the tent in v. 35. Luke uses the same verb when the angel tells Mary the power of the Highest will overshadow her, and again when a cloud overshadows the disciples at the transfiguration.

Hebrews remembers the dedication differently: Moses sprinkled the tabernacle and all its vessels with blood. Exodus 40 speaks only of anointing with oil, while blood appears at the covenant ceremony (24:6–8) and the priests' ordination (Leviticus 8:15, 30). The writer draws them together to argue that almost everything under the law was cleansed with blood.

John sees “the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony” opened in heaven and filled with smoke from God's glory, so that no one could enter until the plagues were finished, an echo of Moses shut out in v. 35. At the end of the book a voice announces that the tabernacle of God is with men and he will dwell with them.
